body.text: This page profiles U.S. R&D tax credit advisors with audit defense teams, including Anchin and KBKG, for businesses claiming the federal I.R.C. §41 research credit. Because examinations turn on technical facts and contemporaneous records, buyers should confirm in writing who will represent them and whether exam, Appeals and Tax Court work and fees are covered.
1. Scope and Method

Where only a firm's own marketing page exists, that is stated, and the firm's statements are reported as its claims, not as independent findings. No firm's staffing, credentials or certifications were confirmed against a third-party registry unless this report says so.

The report does not rank the advisors or recommend one over another. Section 5 sets out analysis drawn from the facts so that a taxpayer can compare advisors on the same terms. Statements of law are limited to the provisions that determine what an R&D audit defense team has to prove, what it costs to defend a claim, and what happens if a claim fails.

body.text: ISO 31000. However, ISO's own ISO 31000 page states that the standard cannot be used for certification purposes, though it can guide internal or external audit programs. The 2009 edition has been superseded: ISO 31000:2018 (edition 2, published February 2018) is the current edition, which ISO reports was reviewed and confirmed in 2023 and is now marked for revision. The International Accreditation Forum resolved in 2017 that there would be no accredited certification to ISO 31000:2009. Alignment with ISO 31000 is therefore a statement of risk-management practice, not a certification.

ISO/IEC 27001 version. Unlike ISO 31000, ISO/IEC 27001 is a certifiable management-system standard, so a buyer can ask for a certificate issued by an accredited certification body and check its scope and expiry date.

Analysis. A buyer should confirm in writing whether defense is included, whether third-party professional fees are covered, whether IRS Appeals is covered, whether an insurer (rather than the firm) stands behind any "insurance" description, and what the mock-audit fee is.

Fee-model wording. Because a fee that depends on the benefit obtained can function like a contingent fee, a buyer should ask the firm to state in the engagement letter exactly how a fixed fee is set and whether any part of it depends on the amount of credit claimed or sustained on audit.
2.3 Anchin

Anchin's R&D audit defense page refers to its R&D Tax Credits team and claims decades of R&D credit audit experience, familiarity with IRS audit techniques, and a reputation for well-documented filings that it says has earned credibility with IRS audit teams. The firm says it will guide clients through IRS audit procedures and help substantiate, clarify and communicate a client's position on exam and at appeals while keeping costs down, and that it can assist whether the original claim was filed by Anchin or another provider. The page names situations it serves: first-time claimants, businesses whose claims were fully denied, clients struggling with contemporaneous documentation requirements, and businesses whose operations changed and need a recalculation. It does not name team members, list specific certifications, or publish pricing.
2.4 KBKG

KBKG's audit defense page describes its technical team as including former IRS engineers and senior analysts, and states that these staff performed audits, examined R&D credits specifically, and trained new IRS engineers in audit techniques. The page names principals (Kevin Zolriasatain, Paul McVoy, Jonathan Tucker, Ian Williams, Bill Taylor, Tetyana Guguchkina) and directors (Jack Jolly, Mark Bodenstab, Michael Maroney, Elise Rhee, Mike Kniss), but does not say which individuals are former IRS staff. It says the firm guides clients selected for an R&D credit audit through the process in the shortest possible time while keeping as much of the credit as possible; a process graphic on the page is not described in text. KBKG offers a free CPE webinar, "R&D Tax Credits & the IRS: How to Prepare for Audit," covering IRS organization, personnel who may be involved in an audit, the history of IRS guidance, typical audit procedures, common problem areas and resolution tools. The page does not address IRS Appeals or state audits and publishes no audit defense fees; it offers a free preliminary analysis of potential credit benefit. KBKG has published commentary on Phoenix Design Group (Section 3.3) authored by Michael Maroney, one of the directors named on the page.
3. Why These Teams Exist: The Legal Standard They Defend
3.1 Qualified research under I.R.C. §41(d)

The credit for increasing research activities is authorized by I.R.C. §41. Under §41(d)(1), as currently in force, "qualified research" means research (A) with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A, (B) which is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature and the application of which is intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, and (C) substantially all of the activities of which constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose described in §41(d)(3). Section 41(d)(3) treats research as conducted for a qualified purpose if it relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability or quality, and never if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic or seasonal design factors. Section 41(d)(2)(B) defines a business component as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula or invention that is held for sale, lease or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business.

Section 174A. The section 174A cross-reference reflects Public Law 119-21 (enacted July 4, 2025), which added §174A. The IRS's Form 6765 instructions confirm that §174A allows a deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures in tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, or an election to capitalize and amortize them over not less than 60 months, and they point to Rev. Proc. 2025-28 for transition options. For earlier tax years, the §41(d)(1)(A) test ran through section 174. An audit defense team defending an older claim must therefore apply the cross-reference in force for the year under examination.

Note on the "four-part test." The statute itself states three conditions plus the section 174/174A link; the "elimination of uncertainty" element derives from the section 174 standard in the Treasury regulations (Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1)) rather than appearing as a separate §41(d)(1) paragraph.

headers: What audit defense teams must document

cells: Specific information the team lacked at the outset of the project regarding capability, method or appropriate design
Reliance on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering or computer science
Identification of each product, process, computer software, technique, formula or invention, and the permitted purpose under §41(d)(3)

Evidence that substantially all (80% or more, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis) of the research activities for each business component were elements of a process of experimentation

body.text: 3.2 Form 6765 disclosure

The IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Revised 12/2025, for use with the January 2025 revision of Form 6765) state that Section G (business component information) is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 and required for tax years beginning after 2025. Section G is not required if either (1) the taxpayer is a qualified small business under §41(h)(3) that checked the box to claim the reduced payroll tax credit, or (2) all of the following are true: total QREs at the controlled-group level on line 48 are $1.5 million or less, average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years are $50 million or less, and the research credit is reported on an original return. The instructions also remind filers that anyone reporting QREs on line 48 must complete Section E.

Analysis. Because the small-claimant exception applies only to original returns, a taxpayer that claims the credit for the first time on an amended return (a refund claim) does not qualify for it, regardless of size. For audit defense purposes, Section G pushes the business-component analysis that a defense team would otherwise assemble during an examination forward to the filing date.
3.3 Court decisions

headers: What it shows for audit defense

cells: 9th Cir., No. 19-55933, argued Nov. 20, 2020, filed Feb. 25, 2021 (unpublished memorandum; "not precedent" except as 9th Cir. Rule 36-3 provides)

The IRS argued the refund claim lacked facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis of the claim (Treas. Reg. §301.6402-2(b)(1)). The majority held the IRS waived that specificity requirement by substantively examining the claim and denying it on the merits after a four-year audit, calling it "a textbook case of waiver." Judge Hunsaker concurred only in the judgment. The Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal and remanded.
Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner
T.C. Memo. 2021-15 (Tax Court Docket No. 17431-17, Judge Halpern); aff'd, 7th Cir., No. 21-3145, argued Oct. 26, 2022, decided Mar. 7, 2023, 62 F.4th 287 (opinion by Judge Brennan)
The taxpayer failed to prove that substantially all (80%+) of its research activities for each business component were elements of a process of experimentation, so none of the expenses qualified.
Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner
T.C. Memo. 2024-113, Docket No. 4759-22, filed Dec. 23, 2024

Credits were denied for sample projects; the court found the firm did not identify the specific information its engineers lacked, and its time records did not support qualified research. Accuracy-related penalties were sustained for the years in which credits were used.

body.text: Harper. The Ninth Circuit ruling is an unpublished memorandum that, by its own terms, is not precedent, and it was decided in the taxpayers' favor on waiver. The specificity standard comes from Treas. Reg. §301.6402-2(b)(1), and IRS Chief Counsel guidance on research credit refund claims sets out the information required, including identification of the business components to which the claim relates.

Little Sandy Coal. It was affirmed by the Seventh Circuit in 2023, which agreed with the result but departed from parts of the Tax Court's reasoning on how the "substantially all" fraction is computed. Applying Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(6), the Seventh Circuit treated the numerator as research activities that are elements of a process of experimentation and the denominator as research activities not excluded by §41(d)(4) whose expenses are deductible under §174. It held, contrary to the Tax Court, that pilot-model production activities can be elements of a process of experimentation and so may belong in the numerator, and it excluded nonproduction wages from the analysis entirely, a change that favored the taxpayer. It agreed with the Tax Court in rejecting a novelty-based approach. The taxpayer still lost because it failed to show that its vessel work followed a scientific-method process, under either treatment of pilot-model costs.

Phoenix Design Group. Commentary on the case reports the court faulted the taxpayer for not identifying, at the outset, the specific information it lacked, and held that uncertainty in one component does not automatically extend to the whole project. Commentary also reports the court gave documentation preference over testimony. Between 2013 and 2016 the taxpayer conducted 409 research projects. The case covered credits generated in 2013–2016 and used in 2015–2019, with accuracy-related penalties assessed for 2015 through 2019. The dispute reached credits generated as early as 2013 because they were carried forward and used in later, still-open years; the generation year's facts were examined when the credit was used.
3.4 Audit timing

The IRS generally has three years to assess tax (the Assessment Statute Expiration Date, or ASED). The IRS states the period runs from the later of the return's due date (including extensions) or the date the IRS received a late-filed return. Under I.R.C. §6501(e), the period extends to six years when a return omits more than 25% of the gross income required to be reported. Under §6501(c), there is no time limit for a false or fraudulent return filed with intent to evade tax, and the period does not begin when no return is filed.

Carryforwards. As Phoenix Design Group shows, a research credit carried forward can be examined in the year it is used, even after the assessment period for the year it was generated has closed. An audit defense team may therefore need contemporaneous records for projects several years older than the return under examination.
4. Cost Exposure Without an Audit Defense Team

That page does not address R&D credits; its tiers are based on general return features such as Schedule C businesses, rental property and Schedule A items. The figures are that one firm's general audit-defense estimates:

Hypothetical example. At $195/hour: 20 × $195 = $3,900. At $395/hour: 20 × $395 = $7,900. The hour count is an assumption for illustration only; no source opened gives a verified average number of hours for an R&D audit.

Penalties if a claim fails. The accuracy-related penalty under I.R.C. §6662(a) is 20% of the portion of the underpayment to which it applies; the civil fraud penalty under §6663(a) is 75% of the portion of the underpayment attributable to fraud. Under §7201, criminal tax evasion carries a fine of up to $100,000 for individuals ($500,000 for corporations), imprisonment of up to five years, or both, together with the costs of prosecution. The general federal sentencing statute, 18 U.S.C. §3571, can raise the maximum fine for a felony to $250,000 for an individual.

Refund claims. Many R&D credits are claimed on amended returns as refund claims. Under I.R.C. §6676, a claim for refund or credit of income or employment tax for an excessive amount carries a penalty of 20% of the excessive amount (the amount by which the claim exceeds what is allowable), unless the excess was due to reasonable cause. The penalty does not apply to any portion already subject to an accuracy-related or fraud penalty under part II of subchapter A of chapter 68. This is the penalty most directly relevant to an R&D refund claim that is disallowed before any refund is paid.

Ten-year credit ban. The statutory ten-year disallowance period is §32(k), which applies to the earned income credit for the 10 taxable years after the most recent year in which a final determination finds the claim was fraudulent (2 years for reckless or intentional disregard of the rules). Parallel bans exist for the child tax credit and the American opportunity tax credit. No equivalent ban was found for the §41 research credit, so this claim should not be applied to R&D credits.
5. Choosing Among Advisors (Analysis)
The following points are analysis drawn from the facts above, not statements of law:

items: Ask what "included" means. Get in writing whether exam, Appeals and Tax Court work are covered, whether third-party professional fees are paid, whether any mock-audit or readiness review carries a separate fee, and whether any "insurance" is issued by a licensed insurer.

Check the team composition. R&D audits turn on technical facts (Phoenix Design Group) and on contemporaneous records (Little Sandy Coal). Ask which named individuals will work the examination and which of them have IRS or litigation experience, since neither firm's page ties those credentials to specific people.
Confirm who can represent you. Ask which team members are attorneys, CPAs or Enrolled Agents, because those credentials determine who can represent the taxpayer before the IRS, including at Appeals.

Treat certification claims carefully. ISO 31000 is not certifiable, and the 2009 edition listed by one firm has been superseded by the 2018 edition. Buyers should ask for certificates only for standards that can actually be certified, such as ISO/IEC 27001, and check the edition and scope.

Plan for Section G. For tax years beginning after 2025, most claimants must report business-component detail on Form 6765, and amended-return claims cannot use the small-claimant exception. This raises the value of advisors who build defensible documentation at filing.

Plan for carryforward exposure. Because carried-forward credits can be examined when used, ask how long the advisor retains project records and whether defense of earlier-generated credits is covered.
